# Digest R4 — Intro 2 Peter + 1:1–2 (L2138–2543)

**Source:** Gene L. Green, *Jude & 2 Peter* (BECNT)  
**Cache:** `R4-intro-2peter-greeting.txt`  
**Range:** L2138–2543  
**Tags:** `2-peter`, `gene-green`, `peter-apostle`, `2-peter-authorship`, `2-peter-jude-relationship`, `jude`, `green-jude-2peter-becnt`

## Coverage

- **L2138–2144** — Authorship intro; self-identification; modern near-universal pseudepigraphy consensus; defenders of authenticity.
- **L2146–2166** — 2 Peter in the early church (Eusebius, 1–2 Clement, Barnabas, Apoc. Pet., Origen, Jerome’s stylistic explanation, canons).
- **L2168–2194** — Contemporary assessment of authenticity (Jude dependence; style/hapax/Hellenistic terms; secretary hypothesis; historical references; anti-gnostic / early Catholicism arguments; personal allusions; Green’s affirmative conclusion).
- **L2196–2238** — Opponents: apostates; moral/doctrinal profile; not same as Jude; not gnostic; not Essene/Balaam-school/pseudoprophets; Neyrey/Epicurean parallels and Green’s counter; amalgam/eclectic identification (four streams).
- **L2240–2312** — Relation to Jude: parallel chart; dependence options; priority of Jude; *imitatio* vs *klopē*; honor of Jude as relative of Jesus.
- **L2314–2360** — Genre and structure: against pure rhetorical outline; against Bauckham testament thesis; genuine letter (advisory/vituperative/paraenetic); outline.
- **L2362–2420** — Green’s full outline of 2 Peter.
- **L2426–2489** — Exegesis of greeting 1:1–2 (Simeon Peter; slave/apostle; isotimos faith; God and Savior; grace and peace; epignōsis); MS note on Simeon/Simon.
- **L2495–2543** — Bridge into body: letter conventions (disclosure formula not testament); body opening as honorific decree (Danker); themes of 1:3–11. (Body opening content begins; range ends at unit outline for 1:3–11.)

**Not in range as separate sections:** Green does not give a freestanding “Date of 2 Peter” essay here; dating arguments are embedded in authorship (second-century gnosticism, early Catholicism, “fathers” of 3:4, Pauline corpus as Scripture). Audience location is argued via 3:1 → 1 Pet. 1:1 (Asia Minor).

## Claims

### Authorship of 2 Peter

1. **Claim (Green):** The author intends readers to recognize 2 Peter as authentic work of the principal apostle Peter.  
   **Quote:** “The author intends that his readers will recognize this letter as an authentic work of the principal apostle, Peter.”  
   **Locus:** L2142

2. **Claim (Green, reporting internal self-presentation):** Author names himself Simeon Peter, slave and apostle; alludes to Transfiguration (1:17–18), imminent demise via Lord’s prophecy (1:14 ≈ John 21:18–19), “second letter” (3:1 = 1 Peter), and parity with Paul (3:15–16).  
   **Quote:** “The author of 2 Peter introduces himself in 1:1 as Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ (“Simeon Peter, slave and apostle of Jesus Christ”). … In 1:17–18 he recalls his experience with the Lord Jesus on the Mount of Transfiguration … consciousness of his imminent demise due to the prophecy given him by the Lord (1:14) … this to be the “second letter” … companion in ministry with Paul … places his own teachings on a par with those of the apostle to the gentiles (3:15–16).”  
   **Locus:** L2142

3. **Claim (Green, reporting scholarly consensus):** Since the early twentieth century, the pseudepigraphical character of 2 Peter has been almost universally recognized; traditional defenses have not received a favorable hearing.  
   **Quote:** “Bauckham (1988c: 3719) states, “The Petrine authorship of 2 Peter has long been disputed, but only since the beginning of this century has the pseudepigraphical character of the work come to be almost universally recognized.” … The arguments forwarded to affirm the authenticity of the letter have not received a favorable hearing, and the failure to convince cannot be fully ascribed to entrenched skepticism.”  
   **Locus:** L2144

4. **Claim (Green, with Bauckham):** Even rejecting Petrine authorship, Bauckham grants better second-century existence evidence than often admitted.  
   **Quote:** “After examining the earliest evidence from the fathers, even Bauckham, who rejects Petrine authorship, states: “There is better evidence than is sometimes admitted for the fact that 2 Peter existed in the second century” (1983: 162).”  
   **Locus:** L2148

5. **Claim (Green):** Evidence for authenticity is weaker than for other accepted writings but stronger than for writings rejected as spurious (citing J. A. T. Robinson).  
   **Quote:** “The evidence in favor of the letter’s authenticity, however, is decidedly weaker than that for any other accepted writing but, on the other hand, stronger than for the writings rejected as spurious (J. A. T. Robinson 1976: 188).”  
   **Locus:** L2148

6. **Claim (Green on Eusebius):** Eusebius places 2 Peter among “disputed books” known to most, not among the spurious Petrine Acts/Gospel/Preaching/Revelation; 2 Peter’s company (James, Jude, 2–3 John) all entered the canon.  
   **Quote:** “He classifies 2 Peter, along with James, Jude, and 2 and 3 John among the “disputed books,” which were “nevertheless known to most” (Eccl. Hist. 3.25.3). Second Peter keeps good company in Eusebius’s list of disputed books since all these documents were finally received into the canon.”  
   **Locus:** L2152

7. **Claim (Green):** 1–2 Clement parallels with 2 Pet. 2:7–10 and 3:4 are best explained by knowledge of 2 Peter, not an unknown apocalyptic source; 1 Clem. calls its source “Scripture,” 2 Clem. “the prophetic word.”  
   **Quote:** “The parallels between 2 Pet. 3:4; 1 Clem. 23.3; and 2 Clem. 11.2 are indeed strong but are best accounted for by the assumption that these letters knew 2 Peter rather than postulating an otherwise unknown apocalyptic source … 1 Clement identifies the written source as “Scripture,” and 2 Clement calls it “the prophetic word.” It is unlikely that some otherwise unknown source would be granted such a high place of honor during this period (cf. 2 Pet. 3:16).”  
   **Locus:** L2154

8. **Claim (Green):** Apocalypse of Peter (ca. 132–135) uses 2 Peter; Bauckham’s use-note “is sufficient to rule out a late date for 2 Peter.”  
   **Quote:** “As Bauckham notes, the use of 2 Peter by the Apocalypse of Peter “is sufficient to rule out a late date for 2 Peter” (1983: 162).”  
   **Locus:** L2158

9. **Claim (Green):** Jerome first explains stylistic discrepancy between 1 and 2 Peter by different interpreters/secretaries; this is the only ancient reason offered for reluctance about authenticity.  
   **Quote:** “Jerome is the first to forward this explanation of the stylistic differences between 1 and 2 Peter. His comment names the reason why some in his era were reluctant to accept 2 Peter as authentic. … Although stylistic issues may not have been the sole reason for the concern about 2 Peter, this is the only explanation offered by any ancient author.”  
   **Locus:** L2164

10. **Claim (Green):** Early evidence is not robust enough to force authenticity, nor weak enough to preclude it; the book was never classified as spurious; acceptance/rejection should not be a test of orthodoxy.  
    **Quote:** “The evidence from the early centuries of the church in favor of the authenticity of 2 Peter is not robust, but neither is it sufficiently weak to preclude the possibility of Petrine authorship. The book was used early and widely and, although doubts did exist, the letter was never classified as spurious … One lesson from antiquity is that acceptance or rejection of the book as authentic should not be a test for orthodoxy.”  
    **Locus:** L2166

11. **Claim (Green, countering Kümmel on Jude):** Dependence on Jude does not exclude Peter if Jude is authentic (half brother of Jesus); *imitatio* of Jude implies Jude’s higher honor as family of Jesus, which explains Peter’s use.  
    **Quote:** “If Jude was truly written by the half brother of Jesus and the brother of James (Jude 1), then 2 Peter could come from the apostolic period. However, since 2 Peter engages in imitatio (μίμησις, mimēsis) of Jude … This dependence places the author of 2 Peter on a level under Jude, a surprising relationship, given the place of Peter in the early church. However, as suggested below, Jude’s place as a member of the family of Jesus gave him a position of special honor within the early church, which would be reflected in Peter’s use of his letter.”  
    **Locus:** L2172

12. **Claim (Green, countering style/Hellenistic vocabulary):** Style, hapax, and Hellenistic terminology do not suffice to reject authenticity; corpus too small to define what Peter could write; Hellenistic terms need not entail Hellenistic conceptual debt; Jewish environment not sealed against Hellenism.  
    **Quote:** “The style and vocabulary of 2 Peter plus the differences between 1 and 2 Peter are not sufficient warrant to reject the authenticity of 2 Peter. We simply do not possess a large enough corpus of Petrine literature to determine what Peter could or could not have written. … The use of Hellenistic terminology as an argument against authenticity is suspect since, though an author may use terms appearing in that milieu, this does not necessarily mean that he was indebted to the concepts as they were framed in that environment … Many of the texts that betray a decidedly “Hellenistic” viewpoint were also quite at home in a Jewish environment, which was not hermetically sealed against Hellenistic language and thought.”  
    **Locus:** L2176

13. **Claim (Green, secretary hypothesis):** Peter needed linguistic help (Mark, Glaucias, Silvanus as amanuensis in 1 Pet. 5:12); Richards’s range (dictation → editing → composition under authorial responsibility) makes it impossible to say what style Peter could not have used; Peter likely approved contents and added final greeting in his own hand.  
    **Quote:** “Given this broad range of secretarial practices, from taking dictation to editing and beyond to composition, it becomes impossible to say what kind of style Peter could or could not have used. … Jerome’s statement, therefore, holds. Peter could have used different secretaries in writing 1 and 2 Peter, and the stylistic features of 2 Peter cannot be invoked as evidence against the letter’s authenticity. We may well suppose, however, that Peter approved the contents and, as was the custom, included the final greeting of the letter in his own hand.”  
    **Locus:** L2178–L2180

14. **Claim (Green, historical-reference counters):** “Fathers” in 3:4 = ancestors, not first Christian generation; “your apostles” (3:2) = those who preached the gospel to the readers in Asia Minor, not exclusion of the author from the apostolate; Pauline collection as “Scripture” (3:16) fits early practice and apostolic status of Paul.  
    **Quote:** “But, as will be argued in the commentary proper, the “fathers” of 3:4 was not a common way to speak of the first generation of Christians but was routinely used both within and outside the Jewish community to refer to ancestors. In 3:2 “your apostles” are simply those who spoke the gospel to the readers of the letter, the apostles who preached in Asia Minor … the collection of Paul’s letters (3:16 and comments) reflects the common practice of copying and collecting letters … That Paul’s letters were regarded as “Scripture” should not surprise us since Paul considered that he was guided by the Spirit and, moreover, he was universally regarded as an “apostle,” an authoritative messenger of Christ.”  
    **Locus:** L2182

15. **Claim (Green, countering second-century gnosticism as authorship argument):** Opponents do not show gnostic dualism, denial of direct creation, or resurrection skepticism; “liberty” and “knowledge” are not gnostic markers in 2 Peter.  
    **Quote:** “Absent is any evidence that the opponents embraced gnostic dualism, with its attendant denial of the direct creation of the material world by God and its skepticism regarding the resurrection. The promise of “liberty” that characterized the heretics is not a marker for gnosticism … Moreover, “knowledge” in 2 Peter is always about personal knowledge of God and Jesus Christ … and at no point does Peter present such knowledge as a counterpoint to a heretical doctrine of gnōsis (Bauckham 1983: 156–57).”  
    **Locus:** L2184

16. **Claim (Green, countering early Catholicism):** 2 Peter does not elevate the episcopal office against heresy; parousia delay discussion is first-century; Peter emphasizes personal knowledge of Christ and reception of the gospel, not mere orthodoxy-as-tenets.  
    **Quote:** “But 2 Peter does not hold up the office of the bishop as the antidote to heresy, nor is discussion about the delay of the parousia itself a marker for early Catholic thought. In fact, questions about the delay of the parousia go back to the first century … Instead of Christianity being crystallized into nothing more than “orthodox doctrinal tradition” … Peter’s emphasis is on the personal knowledge of Jesus Christ and the reception of the gospel (1:2, 8, 12, and comments).”  
    **Locus:** L2186

17. **Claim (Green, on personal allusions / “Simeon Peter”):** Autobiographical details are load-bearing in the argument, not mere pseudepigraphic padding; if pseudepigrapher, odd omissions of Gospel details and presence of “holy mountain”; “Simeon Peter” (1:1) favors authenticity because rarer than “Simon Peter” and not in 1 Peter (which 3:1 shows he knew).  
    **Quote:** “Our author advances his argument by means of these personal allusions … They are threads in the fabric of his argument and not superfluous. … On the other hand, the use of the personal name “Simeon Peter” (1:1) argues in favor of authenticity since it does not appear in 1 Peter (which the author knew, according to 2 Pet. 3:1) and since second-century writers call Peter by this name. Elsewhere in the NT, we hear it for Peter only in Acts 15:14. A pseudepigrapher would have used the more common “Simon Peter.””  
    **Locus:** L2192

18. **Claim (Green, final authorship verdict):** Contemporary objections have weaknesses; early doubts rest mainly on style vs 1 Peter; book dissimilar to later Petrine pseudepigrapha; concerns fit first-century church; “we may reasonably affirm that Simeon Peter, the apostle, authored the book.”  
    **Quote:** “The contemporary objections to Petrine authorship are not without their weaknesses, and we must not allow the volume of opinion to decide the case … The concerns raised within the letter fit well within the struggles of the church of the first century, and we may reasonably affirm that Simeon Peter, the apostle, authored the book.”  
    **Locus:** L2194

### Testament genre debate

19. **Claim (Green, reporting Bauckham’s thesis):** Bauckham’s “testament of Peter” argument (built from Kümmel) became the mainstay against authenticity for many: farewell discourse (1:12–15; 3:1–2) marks pseudepigraphy from a Petrine circle defending apostolic message; mixing future (2:1–3) and past (2:10–22) of heretics shows guise not sustained.  
    **Quote:** “Kümmel identified 2 Peter as a “testament of Peter” (1975: 433; Grundmann 1974: 55–56), and Bauckham developed this observation into the mainstay of his argument against the authenticity of the letter (1983: 159–62; 1988b). … Second Peter presents itself as a farewell discourse of the apostle (1:12–15; 3:1–2) and the adoption of this testamentary genre marks the letter as pseudepigraphic. … The letter, however, mixes prophecies about the coming of the heretics (as in 2:1–3) with references to them in the past tense (as 2:10–22), indicating that the pseudepigrapher could not sustain his guise throughout the whole letter.”  
    **Locus:** L2188

20. **Claim (Green, against Bauckham on genre → pseudepigraphy):** 2 Peter does not follow testamentary conventions and is dissimilar to known testaments; if only testamentary *material* without the genre “testament,” a major anti-authenticity argument falls.  
    **Quote:** “Moreover, as argued elsewhere (see “Genre and Structure,” below), 2 Peter does not follow the conventions of the testamentary genre and is quite dissimilar to known testaments. … If the letter only contains testamentary material but does not belong to the genre of “testament,” one of the major contemporary arguments against the book’s authenticity cannot stand.”  
    **Locus:** L2190

21. **Claim (Green, on tense mixture):** Future/present mixture about false teachers is not clumsy pseudepigraphy; heretics already feast with the church (2:13); M. Green’s parallel with 2 Timothy: future + present stress correspondence of prophecy and event.  
    **Quote:** “Here the question may be raised regarding whether a pseudepigrapher would have been so clumsy on this point, especially since he acknowledges that the heretics are feasting with the church (2:13)—a fact known both to the author and readers! As M. Green (1987: 104n1) observes, a similar combination of present and future tenses when speaking of the false teachers appears in 2 Timothy … and this “combination of future and present is intended to stress the correspondence between prophecy and event. In both cases in 2 Peter where the future is used, it is in immediate juxtaposition to references to the prophets (1:19–2:3; 3:3–4).””  
    **Locus:** L2190

22. **Claim (Green, reporting Bauckham on testament features in 2 Peter):** Bauckham finds miniature homily (1:3–11), testamentary section (1:12–15), and predictions of false teachers (2:1–3a; 3:1–4), claiming contemporary readers would have no doubt of the “testament” genre; since testaments are always pseudepigraphic, 2 Peter cannot be authentic.  
    **Quote:** “In accordance with this genre, 2 Peter includes a “miniature homily” (1:3–11); the testamentary section, which announces Peter’s forthcoming death and his desire to have his teaching remembered (1:12–15); and predictions of the rise of false teachers (2:1–3a; 3:1–4). Bauckham (1983: 132) asserts, “These four passages, but especially 1:12–15, would leave no contemporary reader in doubt that 2 Peter belonged to the genre of ‘testament.’” … Bauckham (1983: 134) concludes that since testaments are always pseudepigraphic, 2 Peter cannot be an authentic work of the apostle Peter.”  
    **Locus:** L2340

23. **Claim (Green, counter to Bauckham):** 2 Peter lacks deathbed scene, burial account, apocalyptic dreams/visions, and blessings/curses typical of testaments; a testamentary *section* does not convert the letter into a testament (cf. Acts 20; 2 Tim. 4; Tob. 14).  
    **Quote:** “Although 2 Peter includes a testamentary section (1:12–15), it lacks the common contours of the testamentary genre. There is no deathbed scene and no final account of the “author’s” burial. … And as J. Charles (1997: 54) notes, “Absent from 2 Peter are apocalyptic dreams and visions and the element of blessings/curses, both of which are salient features of standard testamental genre.” In other words, the inclusion of a testamentary section in 2 Peter (1:12–15) does not convert the letter into a testament.”  
    **Locus:** L2342

24. **Claim (Green):** Neither exhortation nor eschatology is rooted in Peter’s coming demise, but in Transfiguration revelation (1:16–18) and prophetic word (1:19–21)—a distinct departure from testamentary literature’s heavenly-journey basis.  
    **Quote:** “However, the epistle does not link either the author’s exhortations or his eschatology with his coming demise. Rather, he roots his appeal in the revelation given him by the Lord at the time of the transfiguration (1:16–18) and the word of prophetic testimony (1:19–21). This is a distinct departure from testamentary literature.”  
    **Locus:** L2346

25. **Claim (Green):** Call to “remember” is domain of moral exhortation generally, not only testaments.  
    **Quote:** “But the call to “remember” is extremely common in moral exhortation (see Jude 5; 2 Pet. 1:12; 3:1–2; and comments) and is hardly confined to testaments. … Reminders are part of the domain of moral exhortation and not only testaments.”  
    **Locus:** L2348

26. **Claim (Green):** Even if 2 Peter were a testament, that would not necessarily imply pseudepigraphy; in any case the book includes farewell material without testament form. Understanding of genre/structure must be found elsewhere.  
    **Quote:** “In the end, if 2 Peter is a testament, that does not necessarily imply that the book is pseudepigraphic. However, the book includes farewell material and does not share the form or many of the characteristic features of ancient testaments. Our understanding of the genre and structure of the book must be found elsewhere.”  
    **Locus:** L2350

27. **Claim (Green):** The section often called a “testament” (1:12–15) is in fact an epistolary disclosure formula for purpose of writing; letter format is not “literary fiction” framing a testament.  
    **Quote:** “The section identified as a “testament” in 1:12–15 is in fact a form of disclosure formula commonly included in letters to indicate the author’s purpose for writing (White 1986: 30–31, 33, 89, 204). … The letter format is much more than “literary fiction” or simply the frame into which the “testament” of Peter is cast. This is not a sermon or a public discourse dressed as a letter but a genuine correspondence in all respects.”  
    **Locus:** L2506

### Opponents / heresy

28. **Claim (Green):** First readers face internal false teachers (theological and moral), not the external hostility of 1 Peter; danger from within the churches.  
    **Quote:** “Whereas the recipients of the first Petrine Epistle were facing hostility and social rejection because of their faith … those who first heard and read this letter were facing heretical perspectives, both theological and moral, brought into the community by false teachers (2 Pet. 2:1). … The danger appears to have arisen from within the churches and not from outside the gathered Christian communities.”  
    **Locus:** L2198

29. **Claim (Green):** Opponents are real apostates who had experienced salvation and then fell, not people who never were disciples.  
    **Quote:** “These had experienced the salvation of the Lord (2:20a, 21a) but have become “entangled again” in the “defilements of the world” (2:20). … At no juncture does Peter imply that they have somehow never been disciples or that their apostasy is anything other than a fall from grace.”  
    **Locus:** L2200

30. **Claim (Green):** Doctrinal core is skepticism about the parousia and final judgment, resting on apparent delay; they call apostolic preaching “myth” and question prophetic inspiration; they twist Paul; moral error (libertine “freedom”) is joined to this denial of the Master who bought them.  
    **Quote:** “At the heart of the error is their skepticism regarding the coming of the Lord and the divine judgment on the day of the Lord (3:3–10). Their argument is that future judgment will never occur, and they rest their case on the apparent delay in the Lord’s advent (3:4, 9; cf. 2:3). They criticize the apostolic preaching regarding the coming as an invention of the preachers themselves and tag their proclamation as nothing more than “myth.” They even place prophetic inspiration in doubt … Moreover, the heretics have sought support in Paul’s Letters, whose message they have twisted (3:15–16). The doctrinal and moral errors of the false teachers are joined at the hip.”  
    **Locus:** L2204

31. **Claim (Green):** Literary dependence on Jude does not warrant equating the two heretical groups; Peter engages in *imitatio*, adapting Jude to his own ends.  
    **Quote:** “Peter engages in imitatio, which requires that adopters of material adapt it to their own ends instead of slavishly copying, which would have been considered fraud … The intertextual relations between the letters do not warrant equating the two heretical groups.”  
    **Locus:** L2210

32. **Claim (Green):** Situations differ: Jude combats perversion of grace (v. 4); 2 Peter’s immorality rests on negation of parousia/judgment; 2 Peter treats Scripture misuse and prophecy (absent in Jude); Jude’s outsiders with visions/Spirit vs 2 Peter’s internal “false teachers” (not prophets).  
    **Quote:** “The root of the moral problem that Jude combats is a perversion of the doctrine of grace (v. 4). On the other hand, the doctrinal error that is the foundation for the immorality of the opponents in 2 Peter is the negation of the parousia of Christ and future judgment (3:3–10). … the false teachers in 2 Peter present themselves as false teachers and not prophets … The opponents whom Jude faces have entered into the congregation(s) from the outside (v. 4), whereas those that Peter denounces are members of the congregations themselves and enjoy the position of teachers among the believers (2:1, 13 …).”  
    **Locus:** L2212

33. **Claim (Green, against gnostic identification):** Heresy does not conform to any known gnostic system; cosmic dualism, denial of corporeal resurrection, gnostic reading of 2:1, libertinism-from-dualism, and parousia-delay-skepticism all fail; knowledge terms are personal knowledge of God/Christ, not esoteric gnosis.  
    **Quote:** “The heresy confronted in 2 Peter does not conform to any gnostic system known to us, and therefore it is best to lay aside this identification of the heretics as have many contemporary commentators … Although 2 Peter includes repeated references to “knowledge” … Our author instead is concerned about personal knowledge of God and Jesus Christ … At no point does Peter forward this concept as a counterpoint to a heretical view of knowledge (Bauckham 1983: 157).”  
    **Locus:** L2220 (also L2214–L2216 for Käsemann/Kümmel setup)

34. **Claim (Green, against Neyrey’s Epicurean identification as simple identity):** Neyrey’s Epicurean parallels are influential but identification should not be simple; heretics remain in church, affirm creation (3:4) contrary to Epicurus, and their ethics/arrogance/sexual vice are not Epicurean markers; differences underexamined.  
    **Quote:** “We should not simply identify the heretics as Epicureans but may, as Neyrey suggests, recognize in their teaching aspects of Epicurean thought that had much wider currency … If they are Epicureans, we wonder what they are doing within the confines of a Christian gathering that has a decidedly theistic orientation. … We cannot square the false teachers’ claim in 3:4, “Because since the time the fathers died, all things remain as they were from the beginning of creation,” with Epicurean doctrine. … While the similarities between Epicurean philosophy and the position of the false teachers in 2 Peter have been discussed since Neyrey’s work, little attention has been given to the differences that call into question this identification.”  
    **Locus:** L2224–L2230

35. **Claim (Green, positive identification):** Opponents are eclectic “seed-pickers” amalgamating incompatible notions (cf. Acts 17:18; Eclectic movement; Philo on sophists/Balaam): (1) skepticism about predictive prophecy; (2) immutability/eternity of the world (Philo *On the Eternity of the World*; anti-Stoic conflagration); (3) philosophical promise of freedom; (4) sexual immorality and greed; core is apostasy and repudiation of the Lord’s holy commandment.  
    **Quote:** “There were those who could be tagged “seed-pickers” (Acts 17:18), who snatched up philosophical scraps and joined them together in alliance. … We may identify the opponents in 2 Peter as one such group, holding amalgamated beliefs. … A second stream that fed into their views was the question of the immutability of the world, as argued by Adams (2005). … A third stream flowing into the heretics’ teaching is the promise of freedom (2:19) … A fourth stream is their embrace of immoral conduct, especially sexual immorality and greed. … But above all, the heretics are apostates from the faith (2:1, 15, 20–22 and comments), and herein lies the core of their error.”  
    **Locus:** L2232–L2238

### Relation to Jude

36. **Claim (Green):** Substantial parallel language/thought, principally Jude ↔ 2 Pet. 2, also points in chs. 1 and 3; duplicated material in approximately the same order.  
    **Quote:** “Any casual reader of 2 Peter and Jude will notice that a good portion of Jude is found also in 2 Peter. Both the language and thought of these letters are paralleled at numerous points, with the principal locus of these correspondences found between Jude and 2 Pet. 2. … The duplicated material is presented in approximately the same order in both letters.”  
    **Locus:** L2242 (chart L2254–L2286)

37. **Claim (Green, options):** Possible explanations: Jude from 2 Peter (minority/popular); 2 Peter from Jude (vast majority of contemporary commentators); common source; same author (Robinson—least likely).  
    **Quote:** “Several explanations for these parallels are possible. First, it may be that Jude has borrowed his material from 2 Peter … On the other hand, the author of 2 Peter may have borrowed from Jude, an opinion held by the vast majority of contemporary commentators … both Jude and the author of 2 Peter may have drawn upon a common source … The most original suggestion comes from Robinson … both letters were the composition of the same author.”  
    **Locus:** L2296

38. **Claim (Green against common-source and same-author):** Same-author fails on vocabulary/style differences and Jude’s authority to write in his own name; common-source unnecessary if Peter adapted Jude (Ockham); literary dependency and similar ordering strongest.  
    **Quote:** “Robinson’s suggestion is by far the least likely … The differences between the vocabulary and style of these letters argue strongly against this suggestion … The suggestion that both Jude and 2 Peter used a common source is helpful … But we can also account for the differences by assuming that Peter adapted Jude to his own end, and thus there would be no need to postulate an otherwise unknown source. … Literary dependency adequately accounts for all the parallels and is even the strongest argument due to the similar ordering of material in 2 Peter and Jude.”  
    **Locus:** L2298

39. **Claim (Green, priority of Jude):** Against 2 Peter primacy: borrowing was commonplace; Jude more carefully structured (Bauckham); concentration of parallels in 2:1–3:3 argues against Jude using full 2 Peter; early church tended to enlarge not curtail; 2 Peter suppresses Jude’s pseudepigrapha (1 Enoch quote; Michael/Moses). Majority priority of Jude rests on good foundations though not “proven” (Neyrey).  
    **Quote:** “Moreover, as Bauckham (1983: 142) rightly observes, Jude is “a piece of writing whose detailed structure and wording have been composed with such exquisite care, whereas the corresponding parts of 2 Peter, while by no means carelessly composed, are by comparison more loosely structured.” Moreover, the concentration of parallels between these two letters in 2 Pet. 2:1–3:3 argues against the priority of 2 Peter … There is also an attempt on the part of the author of 2 Peter to suppress Jude’s use of pseudepigraphic literature (cf. 2 Pet. 2:10–11 and Jude 8–9 and the absence of the 1 Enoch quotation of Jude 14–15). The majority scholarly opinion regarding the priority of Jude rests on good foundations, but we should mind Neyrey’s judicious comment: “These studies have all added weight to the hypothesis of Jude’s priority by offering convincing interpretations of 2 Peter’s use of Jude, but they have by no means proven it” (1993: 122).”  
    **Locus:** L2300

40. **Claim (Green):** Peter likely has Jude at hand; changes dictate classifying use as *imitatio* (μίμησις), not *klopē*/plagiarism.  
    **Quote:** “In composing his letter, Peter likely has the Epistle of Jude at hand. … The changes he makes from his source dictate classifying this letter in the ancient literary category of “imitation” (μίμησις, mimēsis, imitatio) rather than “theft” (κλοπή, klopē, furtum), or plagiarism, as would be said today.”  
    **Locus:** L2302

41. **Claim (Green on *imitatio*):** Acceptable re-use: rework material as one’s own (Horace, Dionysius, Pseudo-Longinus, Quintilian, Ovid via Seneca); models are “the books,” honored above imitators; best *imitatio* draws from various authors.  
    **Quote:** “Imitatio allowed borrowed material to be reworked extensively to make it one’s own (priuati iuris, according to Horace, Art 131). “‘Theft’ involves derivative copying and is condemned,” but imitatio was “an acceptable, even normal, re-use” (OCD 1188 …). … Those models one would draw from were regarded as “the books,” and due honor is rendered to their authors through this practice of imitatio, or μίμησις (mimēsis). Authors thus imitated were regarded as occupying a greater place of honor than their imitators.”  
    **Locus:** L2304–L2306

42. **Claim (Green):** Peter’s intertextual method transforms Jude for his argument; using Jude highlights Jude’s honor as half brother of the Lord (with James)—structures of early-church honor and authority.  
    **Quote:** “Peter’s intertextual methodology transforms Jude’s thought, making it his own to advance his own argument … the way he uses Jude, however, highlights the honor ascribed to Jude since it recognizes him as one worthy of imitatio. Jude, as the half brother of the Lord, had considerable honor in the early church along with James. … The intertexual relationship between 2 Peter and Jude is not simply a question of sources and comparative linguistic analysis; it also brings us to the core of the sociology of the early church, especially its structures of honor and authority.”  
    **Locus:** L2312

### Date, audience, structure, theology overview

43. **Claim (Green, on date via reception/opponents):** Apoc. Pet. use rules out a late date (per Bauckham); gnostic and early-Catholic second-century framings fail; first-century fit of concerns supports apostolic authorship. (No freestanding absolute year given in this range.)  
    **Quote:** “As Bauckham notes, the use of 2 Peter by the Apocalypse of Peter “is sufficient to rule out a late date for 2 Peter” (1983: 162).” / “The concerns raised within the letter fit well within the struggles of the church of the first century.”  
    **Locus:** L2158; L2194

44. **Claim (Green, audience):** Recipients identified only as people of the faith of equal honor; via 3:1 they are the same as 1 Peter’s audience—most likely Asia Minor provinces (1 Pet. 1:1).  
    **Quote:** “Peter does, however, indicate that the recipients are the same as those who received his first correspondence (2 Pet. 3:1), and therefore they are most likely believers located in the provinces of Asia Minor (1 Pet. 1:1; J. H. Elliott 2000: 84–93).”  
    **Locus:** L2466; also L2354

45. **Claim (Green against rhetorical structuring as primary):** Ancients distinguished letter style from oratory; 2 Peter has markings of a genuine epistle and should be analyzed by epistolography, not Watson’s adjusted rhetorical schema (missing narratio, “faulty” exordium, etc.).  
    **Quote:** “These considerations, among others … caution against adopting Watson’s rhetorical approach in the analysis of 2 Peter. Second Peter has all the markings of a genuine epistle and should be analyzed according to the canons of ancient epistolography.”  
    **Locus:** L2336 (Watson outline L2324–L2334)

46. **Claim (Green against Neyrey’s “literary fiction”):** Epistolary form should not be overshadowed; author himself classifies writing as a “letter” (3:1).  
    **Quote:** “The formal epistolary characteristics of this document should not be overshadowed by another schema but given their full weight. The author himself classifies his writing as a “letter” (3:1), and we can hardly better his evaluation of the genre.”  
    **Locus:** L2352

47. **Claim (Green, letter type):** Combining Demetrius’s advisory + vituperative types; also Libanius’s paraenetic style (persuade/dissuade in friendship); directed to the church, not the heretics (like Jude).  
    **Quote:** “using the taxonomy presented by Demetrius, 2 Peter may be classified as a combination of the advisory and vituperative types. The letter is directed to the church and not to the heretics themselves. … The letter also has characteristics of Libanius’s “paraenetic style,” which was used to persuade or dissuade.”  
    **Locus:** L2358

48. **Claim (Green, structure):** Opening 1:1–2; body 1:3–3:18a (opening 1:3–11; middle 1:12–2:22 with disclosure 1:12–15; closing 3:1–18a with disclosure 3:1–2); doxology 3:18b as brief letter closing focused on God’s eternal honor; liturgical use implied.  
    **Quote:** “After the letter opening (1:1–2), the body of the letter begins (1:3–3:17), which itself may be divided into a body opening, body middle, and body closing (White 1972: 9). The body opening (1:3–11) is the place where “the principal occasion for the letter is usually indicated” (White 1972: 33). The body middle is marked by a transitional formula that discloses the purpose for writing (1:12–15) and runs from 1:12 through 2:22. The body closing is introduced by the transitional formula in 3:1–2 … The body closing ends in 3:18a, with the final doxology in 3:18b serving as a less-than-elaborate letter closing.”  
    **Locus:** L2360; outline L2364–L2420; doxology L2354–L2356

49. **Claim (Green, body-opening theology/themes):** 1:3–11 introduces God’s engagement in salvation (1:3–4), necessity of moral growth (1:5–9), entrance into eternal kingdom (1:10–11), juxtaposed to heretics’ immorality and denial of providence/final judgment; form of honorific decrees (Danker).  
    **Quote:** “In these verses he introduces God’s engagement with the readers in salvation (1:3–4) and underscores the necessity of moral growth (1:5–9) in anticipation of entrance into God’s eternal kingdom (1:10–11). These themes are placed in juxtaposition to the immoral bent of the heretics who assailed the church as they denied the providential care of God as well as the final judgment. The form that the body opening assumes is that of honorific decrees that extol the virtues of certain benefactors (Danker 1978; Danker 1982: 453–67; Neyrey 1993: 150–51).”  
    **Locus:** L2525

50. **Claim (Green on decree form):** Opening like honorific decrees: praescriptio names celebratory community (1:1–2); preamble with Ὡς (= epeidē) + genitive absolute (1:3–4, elliptical); moral resolution 1:5–11 as main clause—period at end of v. 4 wrong; comma preserves decree tone.  
    **Quote:** “Instead of beginning with ἐπειδή (epeidē), Peter’s preamble (1:3–4) opens with the equivalent Ὡς (hōs, because; LSJ 2039), which unfortunately is often left untranslated … We should not, therefore, include a period at the end of verse 4 but rather a comma, leaving a construction that is awkward in English but mirrors the tone of the ancient decrees. After the preamble, such decrees included a resolution, which in 2 Peter’s adaptation of this genre runs from 1:5 through 1:11.”  
    **Locus:** L2533

### I. Greeting 1:1–2

51. **Claim (Green):** Praescriptio follows normal Hellenistic order (author–recipient–greeting), elaborate/theological like other NT letters; “grace and peace” as wish-prayer substitutes for health wish; content modified by gospel.  
    **Quote:** “The epistolary opening, or praescriptio, of 2 Peter is patterned after the style normally found in Hellenistic letters of the era. … In 2 Peter, the greeting “grace and peace” is placed in the form of a wish-prayer, which substitutes for the health wish. While the letter opening would have sounded notes familiar in the day, the content is significantly modified in light of the gospel.”  
    **Locus:** L2437

52. **Claim (Green on “Simeon Peter”):** Συμεών is traditional spelling vs more Hellenized Σίμων; only other NT use for Peter is Acts 15:14 (Palestinian setting); may root author there or show bilingual code-switching; cannot alone prove or disprove authenticity; if authentic, a trace of bilingualism.  
    **Quote:** “The only other place where Peter is called Συμεών (Symeōn) is in the Palestinian setting of Acts 15:14. The use of this name may, therefore, root the author in that setting, although bilingual people could engage in code switching … We can hardly argue either for or against the authenticity of the letter on the basis of the reading Συμεών (Symeōn) … If this is an authentic epistle of Peter, the use of the name Simeon would be a trace of his bilingualism.”  
    **Locus:** L2458

53. **Claim (Green, MS note):** MS evidence slightly favors Σίμων (𝔓72 B Ψ) over Συμεών (א A K P), but not strongly enough; scribes likely harmonized to more common Σίμων.  
    **Quote:** “The MS evidence slightly favors the reading Σίμων (Simōn, 𝔓72 B Ψ) over Συμεών (Symeōn, א A K P) but the testimony of the witnesses is not strong enough to argue for this reading. Likely the scribes sought to harmonize Peter’s name in this text with the more common Σίμων (Simōn) since Συμεών (Symeōn) was used rarely (Acts 15:14).”  
    **Locus:** L2489

54. **Claim (Green):** “Simeon Peter” recalls earliest memory of the fisherman foundational for the church; antiquity and authority adhere to the name and writing under it.  
    **Quote:** “The combined name “Simeon Peter” recalls the earliest memory of the fisherman who became foundational for the life of the church (Matt. 16:16–18). Both antiquity and authority adhere to the name and by extension to this writing composed under that name.”  
    **Locus:** L2460

55. **Claim (Green):** “Slave and apostle of Jesus Christ” stresses divine commission/authority as agent (OT servant-of-the-Lord frame + Roman slave-as-agent), not humility-vs-authority contrast; crucial for uprooting heresy.  
    **Quote:** “Given the way Peter uses “slave” as an agent of the divine Master, the title “apostle” underscores his role as one commissioned by God rather than highlighting the contrast between his humility (“slave”) and authority (“apostle”). The stress is on his divine commission and authority, an important point in his attempt to uproot the heretical elements from the church. The authority of this letter rests not on Peter’s numinous presence in the church but on his role as one whom Christ has sent.”  
    **Locus:** L2462

56. **Claim (Green):** Faith received (λαχοῦσιν) is the gospel allotted by God as portion/inheritance, not mere assent/trust or mere doctrinal summary; related to but wider than “present truth” (1:12); near Jude’s once-for-all tradition (Jude 3).  
    **Quote:** “The “faith” that they have received is the gospel itself and not simply the response of assent and trust nor merely the summary of apostolic doctrine (see Jude 3 and comments). It is not the exact equivalent of the “present truth” (2 Pet. 1:12) but a wider concept. This is the faith that the recipients have “received” as their allotted portion.”  
    **Locus:** L2466–L2468

57. **Claim (Green):** ἰσότιμον = equal honor/dignity with “ours” (apostles/eyewitnesses and wider church); counters heretical incursion; faith is not myth (1:16); catholic embeddedness.  
    **Quote:** “Peter stresses that the faith that God has apportioned these churches is of equal honor to what he and the wider Christian community hold (ἡμῖν, hēmin). It holds the same honor as the faith of the eyewitnesses of the life and glory of Christ (1:16–18; 3:2). Peter is anxious to make the church aware of their embeddedness in the wider Christian community (Neyrey 1993: 147). In this affirmation his emphasis becomes the counterpoint to the incursion of those who are bringing destructive heresies into the church (2:1).”  
    **Locus:** L2470

58. **Claim (Green):** “Righteousness” here is moral impartial justice of apportioning faith equally, not Pauline forensic justification; justice is of “our God and Savior, Jesus Christ.”  
    **Quote:** “Second Peter does not emphasize that “righteousness” by which God justifies the ungodly through faith in Jesus Christ (Rom. 1:16–17; 3:21–26), but its moral quality (2 Pet. 2:5, 21; 3:13). The action of apportioning them a faith of equal honor was an act of divine righteousness or justice. God was completely just or impartial in granting them this faith, not preferring one group (the apostles) over another (the recipients of the letter).”  
    **Locus:** L2472

59. **Claim (Green):** Granville Sharp-type construction: one article τοῦ governs “God and Savior,” both of Jesus Christ (same structure as “Lord and Savior” at 1:11; 2:20; 3:2, 18; cf. Titus 2:13)—clearest NT declarations of Christ’s deity; not evidence of late date (contra Bauckham’s use).  
    **Quote:** “One definite article in the Greek (τοῦ, tou) governs both “God” and “Savior,” which are connected with καί (kai, and). The identical grammatical construction appears elsewhere in the epistle where Jesus Christ is called both “Lord and Savior” (1:11; 2:20; 3:2, 18). … Here, in a construction identical to Titus 2:13 … our author ascribes to Jesus Christ both the titles “God” and “Savior” … This verse is one of the clearest NT declarations of the early church’s conviction of the deity of Christ … The ascription of the divine title to Jesus is hardly evidence for the epistle’s late date (Bauckham 1983: 168–69).”  
    **Locus:** L2472

60. **Claim (Green):** Wish-prayer uses traditional Christian “grace and peace” (vs Jude’s “mercy and peace”); first words identical to 1 Pet. 1:2; grace = saving work + enablement, freely without status (contrast Cicero’s gratia/potentia).  
    **Quote:** “In this prayer, instead of expressing the desire that “mercy and peace” might abound to his readers, as does Jude (v. 2), Peter includes the more traditional Christian “grace and peace” … The first words of the greeting are identical to 1 Pet. 1:2. “Grace” (χάρις, charis) summarizes God’s saving work through Christ Jesus … and embraces the divine enablement given so that his people may do his will … In contrast, God’s grace abounds to people freely without regard to status and is even given to those who are guilty (Rom. 5:20–21) and God’s enemies (Rom. 5:10).”  
    **Locus:** L2476

61. **Claim (Green):** “Peace” = messianic salvation / peace with God, not emotional tranquillity; multiplication of grace/peace introduces moral-progress theme (1:5–9; 3:18) over against heretics; growth is fruit of divine initiative.  
    **Quote:** “Peter’s and other NT authors’ concern is not with an experience of “peace” or emotional tranquillity but rather with “peace” with God (Rom. 5:1), which constitutes salvation. … The epistle demonstrates a particular interest in moral progress of the believers (2 Pet. 1:5–9; 3:18), and this growth and stability in the faith is placed over against the influence of the heretics. Whatever progress they experience is, however, fruit of the divine initiative. The epistle’s theme of moral progress is introduced here in the opening wish-prayer.”  
    **Locus:** L2478

62. **Claim (Green):** ἐπίγνωσις / γνῶσις density is not evidence of second-century gnostic combat; opponents mixed philosophic perspectives with Christian teaching; epignōsis here is personal knowledge of God and Jesus (genitive of the one known); God’s benefits never detached from his person.  
    **Quote:** “The ubiquitous presence of the various forms of “knowledge” and “to know” and the critique of “false knowledge” are not evidence that the epistle combats the gnostic heresy of the second century … Peter’s opponents were others, most likely those who mixed various philosophic perspectives with Christian teaching … This personal knowledge is in mind here, and the genitive τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν … identifies the one known … In this personal knowledge of God, the great privilege of Christianity, these believers may abound in saving grace and peace. God’s benefits are never detached from his person.”  
    **Locus:** L2480–L2482

63. **Claim (Green):** V. 1 ascribes “God” and “Savior” to Jesus; v. 2 differentiates God (the Father) from Jesus “our Lord”—raw building blocks for trinitarian theology (Spirit not named here).  
    **Quote:** “While verse 1 ascribes the titles “God” and “Savior” to Jesus Christ, here God is differentiated from Jesus, and we should understand Peter’s thought to mean “God the Father” (1 Pet. 1:2). Within these verses we find the raw building blocks for trinitarian theology, although the Holy Spirit is not named in this verse (cf. 1 Pet. 1:2).”  
    **Locus:** L2484

## Extractor notes

- **Claim count:** 63 claims, all attributed to **Gene L. Green** with verbatim anchors and LINE loci from the assigned cache range.
- **Critical controversy material extracted:** counters to Bauckham testament thesis (claims 19–27); secretary hypothesis (13); “Simeon Peter” (17, 52–54); literary dependence direction + *imitatio* (36–42); opponent identification not gnostic (15, 33, 62) and not simple Epicurean (34–35).
- **Date:** No standalone date essay in range; dating woven through authorship/reception (claims 8, 15–16, 43).
- **Range end:** L2543 ends at outline labels for body opening 1:3–11; decree/body-opening claims (49–50) are within range via L2525–L2539.
